paragraphs.text: March 23. The martyrdom of Saint Dometius and his disciples.

Julian then arrived in the city of Antioch—for he should not be called emperor. It is enough to call him a lawless man and a transgressor, since he transgressed God's commandments and sacrificed to idols. For he had been instructed in the words of God and had been appointed a deacon among the clergy. He had carried the most pure Mysteries and stood ministering in the sanctuary. He abandoned his rank—or rather, he did not abandon it, but God brought him to disgrace as unworthy, because he had imitated Judas's deceit [?]. So, upon entering the city of Antioch, he persecuted the devout, while he cherished and supported those who persecuted them. Others he compelled to deny God, thus fulfilling what the apostle said: “Wicked people and sorcerers will go from bad to worse, deceiving through their deceptions.” But those who stood upon the firm rock mocked him. For this man was not simple and ignorant, but cunning, using glory and wealth to deceive the souls of those built upon sand. So he entered the city, and the great church that Emperor Constantine had built he reviled and dishonored,

making it a stable for horses and setting the sanctuary apart as a place for his own horse to stand. Such were the many evils he inflicted upon God's honored church. Then war arose against that impious man from Assyria, and he had to go and fight. He set out for war, and as he was traveling along the road, some people approached him and brought accusations against the righteous Dometius. The tyrant gladly received these accusers and answered, saying, “Go and bring him to me.” Hearing this, those wretched men rejoiced and praised the tyrant, so that his rage against the Christians would remain firm and unrelenting. They ran to the cave of Saint Domitian and saw him looking like an angel, standing with his hands stretched out toward heaven and offering a song of thanksgiving to God, together with his two disciples. At first they were struck with awe and said to one another, “How can we approach such a martyr [?]? Or what charge can we find to bring about his destruction? Will we not bring sin upon ourselves?” But others said, “Let us drive him out of these lands.”

“What if he draws all the people to himself, and they believe in the one born of Mary, whom the Jews once crucified with two robbers, as someone deserving death?” The emperor, the nobles, and the princes were angry with the Christians. “Who [?] to kill this man? Come, then, let us see what they are.” And when they went up to that holy man, they saw him standing with his two disciples, saying the prayer of the sixth hour. And they said to him, “Come out; prepare to travel to the emperor.” But he did not answer them and continued in his prayer. And again they said to him, “Come out; prepare to travel [?] to the emperor, for he is coming here.” But he, unwilling to leave his prayer, did not answer them a word. Immediately, like bloodthirsty lions, they rushed at him, gnashing their teeth, and picked up stones and threw them at him and at both his disciples. Those godless men threw so many stones at the righteous man that they filled the cave with stones, so that the cave could no longer be recognized. And thus the holy man surrendered his soul

to the Lord, together with his two disciples. And that cave became the tomb of the righteous man and his disciples. Those who had killed the righteous man ran and reported everything that had happened to Emperor Julian, saying, “We have killed the righteous man.” Oh, that lawless fury! Oh, the blindness at that time of the unbelieving people who killed the faithful and sought to defile righteousness with blood, striving and searching everywhere to kill the worker of godliness! But leaving aside this fury of those godless men against the godly, I will return to the account of Saint Domitian. The site of the holy man’s cave was obliterated and became unknown, covered with the stones they had thrown at the righteous man. It became overgrown with thick vegetation and thorns. For to this very day, that mountainside remains overgrown. When two years had passed after the holy man’s death, a certain merchant happened to drive his camels there and pasture them in that place. While the camels were grazing there, one of them happened to go down near the village and enter a field,

wanting to eat. When the owner of that field saw it, he ran to drive it out. As it was being driven out, it fell into a [?]. and broke its front leg. And a dispute arose between the owner of the camel and the owner of the field. He abandoned it in the hills, at the place where the holy man lay, unseen by anyone. Its owner then went to the city of Cyrrhus and told the governor about the field and how they had crippled his camel. The camel was left there for four days, lying in that place and trying to get up, but unable to steady its broken leg. It took a step, and its leg went into an opening in the cave where the relics of the saints were. Immediately the camel’s leg became firm and sound. When its owner arrived, he hurried toward it. When the camel saw him, it pulled its leg free and ran to meet him. When he saw it, he was astonished and praised and glorified the Lord. His companions asked him, “What is this marvelous thing?” He told them, “I left it lame in that place.” They said to him, “Come and show us, so that we may see the place more clearly.” And they went to the place

and found a large opening. Immediately some of them said to him, “Truly, this is the place of Saint Dometius. Here, then, we shall also find his holy relics.” They went and brought priests to offer prayers at the place. They took hoes and spades and dug. When they found the relics, they brought them out with songs and praises and with fitting honor, and carried them into the church of the village there. A large crowd gathered, intending to seize the relics of the righteous man and of his disciple. They rebuked them as troublemakers. But those who loved the saints took their relics and laid them in a holy place. There was a great celebration in those regions. For everyone gathered together—priests and clerics, laypeople and monks, and abbots—and held a great celebration. They observe the commemoration of the holy relics even to this day. This is the life of Saint Dometius. This is the martyrdom of the righteous man. These are the labors of the venerable man, pleasing to God and to the fathers and angels and people. Because of these things he is especially beloved by God, honored by princes, and venerated by priests
and devout people. He also has the boldness to pray to God for us. To him be glory and dominion, together with the Father and the Holy Spirit, now and always and forever and ever. Amen.
